Injurious
in-JOO-ri-us
adj. (insolent; violently insulting; one who outrages others)
Greek hubristes, an insolent man — the noun behind the English hubris, meaning one who treats others with contemptuous violence for the pleasure of it. The Authorized Version's injurious carries the older English force of one who does injury, not merely one who is harmful.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief. Paul is describing himself, and the three words mount. A blasphemer sins against God directly. A persecutor pursues God's people. Injurious is the strongest of the three and the least understood in modern English, because it now suggests something merely harmful. The Greek hubristes means an insolent man — one who inflicts outrage on others with contempt, who enjoys the humiliation he causes. Luke records the fact behind the word: Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord. Paul does not soften the self-description anywhere in his letters, and he returns to it as the measure of what he received: this is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. The clause about ignorance is not an excuse, and it must not be read as one. Paul says he obtained mercy, which is precisely what a man with an excuse does not need; and he says he did it in unbelief, which names the ignorance as culpable. His point is that the mercy reached the worst case on record, so that no sinner after him may plead his own case is beyond it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): wrongful; unjust; hurtful; doing or occasioning injury; given to injuring others; contumelious.

expand to see more

INJURIOUS, a. Wrongful; unjust; as an injurious proceeding.

INJURIOUS, a. Hurtful; mischievous; occasioning injury or damage.

INJURIOUS, a. Contumelious; reproachful; abusive; as injurious language.

BLASPHEMER, n. One who blasphemes; one who speaks of God in impious and irreverent terms.

PERSECUTOR, n. One that persecutes; one that harasses others with continued cruelty for adhering to a particular religion.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 1:13 — "Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief."

1 Timothy 1:15 — "This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief."

Acts 9:1 — "And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,"

1 Timothy 1:12 — "And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry;"

Modern Corruption

The clause about ignorance is regularly turned into a doctrine of diminished responsibility, and Paul's self-description into rhetorical humility; he means both literally, and the mercy is the greater for it.

expand to see more

Because I did it ignorantly in unbelief is pressed into service for a general principle that sin committed in ignorance is not properly guilt — a principle that would empty the doctrine of original sin and much of Romans 1, where men who did not like to retain God in their knowledge are without excuse. Paul is not pleading extenuation. He says in the same breath that he obtained mercy, and mercy is what is shown to the guilty. Unbelief is itself named as the condition of the ignorance, and unbelief is sin. What Paul offers is not a lighter verdict on his past but an explanation of why grace, and not justice, met him on the Damascus road.

A second and gentler distortion treats of whom I am chief as a pious overstatement — the sort of thing a humble man says. The present tense forbids it: not was chief but am. Paul, years into an apostolic ministry, still reckons himself the chief case, because he had been a hubristes, a man who outraged the saints with contempt. The doctrinal use he makes of it is exact and pastoral: if the worst was received, the pattern holds for all who come after. Reduce the self-description to modesty and the argument it was built to carry falls apart.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hubristes (G5197), an insolent and violent man; blasphemos (G989), a blasphemer; diokes (G1376), a persecutor; eleeo (G1653), to obtain mercy.

expand to see more

Greek hubristes (G5197) — an insolent man who outrages others; rendered injurious, and elsewhere despiteful.

Greek blasphemos (G989) — a railer, a blasphemer; the first term of Paul's three.

Greek diokes (G1376) — a persecutor; its only occurrence, of Paul himself.

Greek eleeo (G1653) — to receive mercy; the verb that answers all three terms.

Greek agnoeo (G50) — to be ignorant; qualified here by in unbelief, which names it as culpable.

Usage

"“a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious” — three terms, mounting."

"“but I obtained mercy” — what the guilty receive."

"“of whom I am chief” — present tense, years into the ministry."
